div.div: Operational Transformation — send intents, and transform them against each other

div.div:
The server picks an order, then TRANSFORMS the second op
against the first: B’s insert at 3 becomes an insert at 4,
because A already put a character there.

div.div:
Needs a central server to decide the order — that is the
cost. Simple ops, small payloads, and the algorithm is
notoriously easy to get subtly wrong.

div.div:
Both insert after the same character. The tie is broken by
comparing ids — deterministically, the same way on every
replica. No server has to arbitrate.

div.div:
Works peer-to-peer and offline. Costs metadata per
character — a mature library (Yjs, Automerge) keeps that
manageable; a hand-rolled one will not.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 756px; height: 1px; padding-top: 501px; margin-left: 40px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: var(--dg-warn-fg);

display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans',-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif; color: var(--dg-warn-fg); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: Never hand-roll either. The honest answer is "Yjs or Automerge, because OT is famously easy to get subtly wrong and a bad merge silently destroys someone's work". Reach for OT only if you must interoperate with an existing OT server.

div.div: The parts a library does NOT give you, and every one is a follow-up: presence and remote cursors · undo that only undoes YOUR edits · awareness of who is typing · access control · persistence and compaction of the operation log · and what the document looks like to someone who joins an hour late.
